mainTopic: Who must bring proof about a new wife's blemishes, and שמואל's parallel ruling about a cow swapped for a donkey
overview: The משנה teaches that if blemishes are found while the girl is still in her father's house, the father must prove they appeared after אירוסין. If they are found after she entered her husband's home, the husband must prove they were there before. The גמרא explains the סיפא by counting presumptions: the woman has two and the husband has one, so the husband must prove his claim. If the husband proves the blemish existed before אירוסין, the count flips. No one accepts blemishes, and the money stays where it is, so he wins. רב אשי offers a different explanation: in the רישא the money would go to her father, while in the סיפא she claims for herself. רב אחא challenges him from a ברייתא about רבי מאיר. The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is about an extra finger or toe, where the father's only possible proof is that the husband saw it and accepted it. The גמרא then brings שמואל's ruling about a cow swapped for a donkey that died, and says the משנה teaches the same idea about a bride. It begins to ask which bride case is meant, and the answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: One presumption cannot beat two
steps.stepSummary: In the סיפא, the husband's one חזקה stands against the woman's two, so the woman wins.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is one presumption against two, and we do not follow one presumption against two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its explanation of the סיפא of the משנה. The husband has only one presumption on his side, and the woman has two, so his one does not win.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the husband's side is חזקת ממון: money stays with whoever holds it. On the woman's side are two: her body is presumed to stay as it was (no blemish until proven), and a man does not 'drink from a cup' without checking it first. Two presumptions together beat one, so the husband must bring proof.

keyTerms.meaning: One against two: one presumption opposed by two others
A presumption; what we assume to be true unless it is proven otherwise
We do not say; we do not rule that way

phrases.english: It is one presumption in place of (against) two,
phrases.notes: The one is the husband's claim to keep his money; the two are on the woman's side.

phrases.english: and we do not follow one against two.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲדָא בִּמְקוֹם תַּרְתֵּי, וַחֲדָא בִּמְקוֹם תַּרְתֵּי לָא אָמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer begun on the previous daf explaining why the סיפא puts the burden on the husband.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the סיפא the woman has two presumptions against the husband's one, so the husband must bring proof.

steps.title: What if the blemish is proven to come before the betrothal?
steps.stepSummary: If the husband proves the blemish was there before אירוסין, the body presumption is gone. Only the 'cup' presumption is left for the woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he proves she had it before she was betrothed, we can no longer say 'leave the body in its presumed state.' What is left? Only the presumption that a person does not drink from a cup unless he checks it first, so this man must have seen the blemish and accepted it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now looks at the case where the husband brings proof that the blemish existed before אירוסין. It asks what argument the woman still has left. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the husband proves the blemish was already there, the woman loses her body presumption, because we now know her body was blemished. The only argument she has left is the 'cup' presumption: he must have checked her, seen the blemish, and accepted it.

keyTerms.meaning: Before she was betrothed
Leave the body in its presumed state: assume no blemish until proven

keyTerms.term: אֵין אָדָם שׁוֹתֶה בְּכוֹס אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן בּוֹדְקוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: A person does not drink from a cup without checking it first; a man checks a woman before marrying her
He saw it and accepted it (made peace with it)

phrases.english: If he proves the blemish was there before she was betrothed,

phrases.aramaic: הַעֲמֵד הַגּוּף עַל חֶזְקָתוֹ לָא אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר.
phrases.english: we cannot say 'leave the body in its presumed state.'
What is left for her?
The presumption that a person does not drink from a cup
unless he checks it first,
and so this man saw the blemish and accepted it.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד שֶׁלֹּא תִּתְאָרֵס — הַעֲמֵד הַגּוּף עַל חֶזְקָתוֹ לָא אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר. מַאי אִיכָּא?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ordinary סיפא case to the case where the husband has proof of an early blemish.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: With the body presumption gone, what argument does the woman still have?

steps.title: On the contrary: no one accepts blemishes
steps.stepSummary: The 'cup' argument is cancelled by the presumption that people do not accept blemishes, and the money stays with the husband.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary: there is a presumption that a person does not accept blemishes. So we leave the money with the one who holds it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against the woman's last argument. Her 'cup' presumption is now one against the husband's two (no one accepts blemishes, plus the money stays where it is), so he keeps the money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'cup' presumption says he checked her and accepted what he saw. The גמרא answers with an opposing presumption: a man who saw blemishes would not have accepted them. Together with חזקת ממון (the money stays with whoever holds it), the husband now has two presumptions against her one, so he does not pay the כתובה.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary; the opposite is true
Accepts blemishes, makes peace with them
Leave the money where it is: whoever holds it keeps it

steps.whatToRemember: In the סיפא the woman wins (two presumptions against one). If the husband proves the blemish came before אירוסין, he wins: no one accepts blemishes, and the money stays with him.

phrases.aramaic: אַדְּרַבָּה: חֲזָקָה אֵין אָדָם מִיפַּיֵּיס בְּמוּמִין,
phrases.english: On the contrary: there is a presumption that a person does not accept blemishes,
so leave the money in its presumed place (with the husband).

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּרַבָּה: חֲזָקָה אֵין אָדָם מִיפַּיֵּיס בְּמוּמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the 'he saw and accepted' argument raised in step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the woman's last remaining argument, the 'cup' presumption.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It is met by the opposing presumption that people do not accept blemishes, and together with חזקת ממון the husband has two presumptions against her one.

steps.title: רב אשי: whose money is being claimed?
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains the difference between the רישא and the סיפא differently. In the רישא the money belongs to the father; in the סיפא it belongs to the woman herself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: the רישא is like saying 'my father has a hundred in your hand,' and the סיפא is like saying 'I have a hundred in your hand.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a new, different way to explain why the רישא and the סיפא of the משנה have different rules.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the רישא she is still in her father's house, so the כתובה money would go to her father. She is claiming for someone else, and her body presumption does not help someone else's claim. In the סיפא she is married and claims for herself, so her body presumption does help her.

keyTerms.meaning: The first part of the משנה
The last part of the משנה
'You hold a hundred that belongs to my father': a claim on someone else's behalf
'You hold a hundred that belongs to me': a claim for oneself

steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי is not adding to the 'one against two' explanation. He is offering a completely different reason for the difference between the רישא and the סיפא.

phrases.english: רב אשי said:
The first part is like 'my father has a hundred in your hand,'
phrases.notes: A מנה is a hundred dinars. In the first part she is still in her father's house, so the money would go to him.

phrases.english: and the last part is like 'I have a hundred in your hand.'

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: רֵישָׁא ״מָנֶה לְאַבָּא בְּיָדְךָ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the contradiction between the רישא and the סיפא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases by whose money is being claimed
steps.terutzMaskana: The body presumption only helps a person claiming for herself, not for her father.

steps.title: Challenge from רבי מאיר's admission
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that even for a married woman, the father must prove certain blemishes. That seems to be an 'I have a hundred' case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא son of רב אויא challenged רב אשי: רבי מאיר agrees that for blemishes that would normally come with her from her father's house, the father must bring proof. But why? It is an 'I have a hundred in your hand' case!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא attacks רב אשי's explanation using a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is about a woman already married, so by רב אשי's rule she claims for herself and her body presumption should protect her. Yet the ברייתא puts the burden on her side for blemishes that come from her father's house. That seems to contradict רב אשי.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי מאיר agrees (in this one case)
Blemishes that would normally have come with her from her father's house
But why?

phrases.aramaic: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha son of Rav Avya challenged Rav Ashi:
Rabbi Meir agrees regarding blemishes
that would normally come with her from her father's house,
that the father must bring proof.
But why? It is an 'I have a hundred in your hand' case!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב אשי's explanation from step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's rule that a married woman claims for herself and is protected by her body presumption
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא puts the burden of proof on the father even though she is married and the claim is her own.

steps.title: The ברייתא means an extra finger or toe
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about an extra finger or toe, which she was clearly born with.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? An extra finger or toe.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the ברייתא to one specific kind of blemish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An extra finger or toe is something a person is born with, so the body presumption cannot help her. Everyone knows it was there before אירוסין. רב אשי's rule still holds for ordinary blemishes.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)
An extra finger or toe

phrases.english: What case are we dealing with here? An extra finger or toe.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the ברייתא to a specific case
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא covers only a blemish she was born with, where the body presumption does not apply.

steps.title: What proof could the father bring?
steps.stepSummary: If the blemish is clearly from birth, what could the father possibly prove?
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is an extra finger or toe, what proof could he bring?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is puzzled. It cannot be proven that an extra finger grew later, so what proof does the ברייתא mean?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says 'the father must bring proof,' which suggests there is something he could prove. With a blemish from birth, he cannot prove it appeared after אירוסין, so the proof must be about something else.

keyTerms.meaning: What proof can he bring?

phrases.english: If it is an extra finger or toe, what proof can he bring?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how the answer in step 6 fits the words 'bring proof.'
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the father's proof could be about, when the blemish is clearly from birth

steps.title: Proof that the husband saw it and accepted it
steps.stepSummary: The father can prove that the husband saw the extra finger or toe and accepted it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Proof that he saw it and accepted it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the father's proof is not about when the blemish started, but that the husband knew about it and accepted it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally we assume no one accepts blemishes. If the father brings witnesses that the husband saw the extra finger or toe and still went ahead, the husband cannot complain, and the כתובה must be paid.

keyTerms.meaning: Proof, usually through witnesses

steps.whatToRemember: רב אשי's rule stands. The ברייתא is about an extra finger or toe, where the only possible proof is that the husband saw it and accepted it.

phrases.english: Proof that he saw it and accepted it.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The father proves that the husband saw the blemish and accepted it before marriage.

steps.title: Swapping a cow for a donkey when the donkey dies
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that if a cow and donkey were swapped and the donkey died before the cow's owner pulled it, the donkey's owner must prove the donkey was alive when the cow was pulled.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: Two people swapped a cow for a donkey. The donkey's owner pulled the cow, but the donkey died before the cow's owner pulled the donkey. The donkey's owner must bring proof that his donkey was still alive at the moment the cow was pulled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from שמואל about a swap where one animal died and nobody knows exactly when.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pulling the cow (משיכה) is what makes the swap take effect, so the cow's owner becomes owner of the donkey at that moment. If the donkey was alive then, it died as the cow-owner's property. If it was already dead, there was nothing to swap. שמואל puts the burden of proof on the donkey's owner, even though he is the one who already pulled the cow and holds it.

keyTerms.meaning: One who swaps or trades one item for another (חליפין)
Pulled, a way of acquiring an animal (משיכה)
Did not manage to, did not get the chance to
To bring proof, to carry the burden of proof
Alive, still in existence

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume the person holding the cow keeps it. The donkey's owner already pulled the cow, but שמואל still says he must prove his case.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling about who must prove what in a case of doubtful timing is the model the גמרא will now compare to a case in our משנה.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
One who swaps a cow for a donkey,
and the owner of the donkey pulled the cow,
phrases.notes: Pulling the cow is what makes the whole swap happen. Once he pulls it, the donkey automatically belongs to the other person.

phrases.english: but the owner of the cow did not manage
to pull the donkey
before the donkey died —
the owner of the donkey must bring proof
that his donkey was alive
at the time the cow was pulled.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל הַמַּחֲלִיף פָּרָה בַּחֲמוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of who must prove a woman's blemishes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When it is unclear whether the donkey died before or after the cow was pulled, the donkey's owner must prove the donkey was alive at the moment of pulling.

steps.title: The משנה teaches the same idea with a bride
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה adds that the תנא of the משנה taught the same principle in a case involving a כלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the תנא taught the same thing about a bride.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה says שמואל's ruling has a source: the משנה teaches the same idea in a case about a bride.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claim is that a case about a bride follows the same logic as the cow and donkey. In both cases something is found wrong and we do not know whether it happened before or after the deal took effect. Which bride case this is has not been said yet.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא, the teacher of the משנה, taught (this idea)
A bride

phrases.english: And the tanna taught a bride.
phrases.notes: He means the משנה already taught this same idea in the case of a bride.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connects שמואל's ruling to a case in the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's ruling that the donkey's owner must prove the donkey was alive when the cow was pulled.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A case in the משנה involving a כלה, not yet identified.

steps.title: Which bride case is meant?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which case of a bride in the משנה supports שמואל, and begins to propose an answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which bride case? If you say...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which bride case רב יהודה was talking about. It starts to suggest one with "If you say," which sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה has more than one case about a woman whose blemishes are found. The גמרא needs to find the one that matches the cow-and-donkey logic. The word אילימא signals that the first suggestion is coming, and that it may well be rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: Which one?
If you say, which opens a suggested answer that is often rejected

phrases.english: Which bride?
If we say

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the exact source behind רב יהודה's claim in step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case of a bride in the משנה follows the same principle as שמואל's cow-and-donkey ruling.
